\chapter{From, Until, and Instead}
\label{ch:hi-safar}
\hlchaptermodality{102}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say a span of days or hours with a marker on each end, name a second way of travelling, and correct somebody's guess by naming the option they got wrong and then the right one.}

Read the correction a practice paper prints -- bas se nahiin, tren se -- and say which side of the negative holds the true answer, then tell a span se from a means se in one sentence carrying both.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tak]{\hi{तक} — where it stops}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-tak}



\begin{quote}
Say the word that marks where something comes \textbf{from}. Then say \emph{at five o'clock}. One of those two words has been doing its job alone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{तक}}
\textbf{\hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक}} — until five o'clock.

\textbf{\hi{से}} marks a \textbf{start}. \textbf{\hi{तक}} marks a \textbf{stop}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it marks} \\
\midrule
\hi{से} & the point something begins at \\
\hi{तक} & the point something ends at \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are \textbf{postpositions}, so both come \textbf{after} the word they attach to. English puts \emph{until} in front and Hindi puts \textbf{\hi{तक}} behind, and that is not a quirk of this word — it is the same fact about the language that put \textbf{\hi{के}} in the middle of every phrase in the last chapter.

\textbf{\hi{तक}} also stretches across space, not only time: \textbf{\hi{घर} \hi{तक}} is \emph{as far as the house}. One word covers both, because a stopping point is a stopping point whether you measure it in hours or in streets.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it does not have to be a pair}]
\textbf{\hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक}} on its own is a complete and ordinary thing to say. It names only the end, and leaves the beginning to be understood — usually \emph{now}.

That matters because the next lesson pairs the two words, and a reader who has only ever seen the pair will not recognise \textbf{\hi{तक}} standing by itself on a sign or in a notice, which is where it most often appears.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{घर} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of \textbf{\hi{से}} and \textbf{\hi{तक}} marks the end
  \item which side of its noun a Hindi postposition stands on
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{तक}} mark? (The stopping point.) Where does it stand? (After its word.) Does it need \textbf{\hi{से}} to be present? (No.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[somvār se śukravār tak]{\hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक} — a span, marked at both ends}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-se-tak-din}



\begin{quote}
Say the first and last weekdays of the working week. Then say the word that marks a stopping point.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{से} … \hi{तक}}
\textbf{\hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक}} — from Monday to Friday.

Two days, and \textbf{each one carries its own marker}.

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
\hi{सोमवार} \textbf{\hi{से}} & start here \\
\hi{शुक्रवार} \textbf{\hi{तक}} & stop here \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English builds a span out of \emph{from} and \emph{to} standing \textbf{in front of} their days. Hindi builds it out of \textbf{\hi{से}} and \textbf{\hi{तक}} standing \textbf{behind} theirs.

The shape looks harder than it is, because both halves are already familiar and neither is doing anything new. What is new is only that \textbf{they are allowed to appear together}, and that when they do, the whole thing is one idea rather than two.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: order is not optional}]
The \textbf{\hi{से}} half comes first. Always, and for the same reason English says \emph{from Monday to Friday} and not the other way round: a span is told in the direction it runs.

What Hindi does \textbf{not} copy is the position of the markers. Read the pair as two small packages rather than as one long phrase:

\textbf{{[} \hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} {]} {[} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक} {]}}

Read it that way and a longer span — a written account of somebody's week — comes apart at the right seams the first time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the marker the first day carries
  \item the marker the last day carries
  \item which half of the span is said first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many markers does a Hindi span carry? (Two — one on each end.) Where do they stand? (After their days.) Which end is named first? (The start.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[subah se śām tak]{\hi{सुबह} \hi{से} \hi{शाम} \hi{तक} — the same frame, smaller units}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-se-tak-samay}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{morning} and \emph{evening}, the two Persian loanwords you met early on. Then guess how a span between them is built.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सुबह} \hi{से} \hi{शाम} \hi{तक}}
\textbf{\hi{सुबह} \hi{से} \hi{शाम} \hi{तक}} — from morning until evening.

If you guessed, you guessed right. Nothing about the frame changed.

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what is spanned} & \textbf{Hindi} \\
\midrule
days & \hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक} \\
parts of a day & \hi{सुबह} \hi{से} \hi{शाम} \hi{तक} \\
clock hours & \hi{दस} \hi{बजे} \hi{से} \hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three different units, one frame. \textbf{\hi{से}} and \textbf{\hi{तक}} do not care what they are attached to, and that is worth noticing because English does not always manage it either — \emph{from ten to five} is fine, but \emph{from Monday until Friday} and \emph{until the house} pull on different senses of the same word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the clock row is two packages, not four words}]
\textbf{\hi{दस} \hi{बजे} \hi{से}} is one package and \textbf{\hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक}} is another. Each already had its own marker — \textbf{\hi{बजे}} — before the span marker arrived, so the clock row stacks \textbf{two} postposition-like endings on one side.

Read it inside out:

\textbf{\hi{दस}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{दस} \hi{बजे}} (\emph{at ten}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{दस} \hi{बजे} \hi{से}} (\emph{from ten})

Nothing is being negotiated between them. Each step adds one word to the right of what came before, which is the direction this language always builds in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{सुबह} \hi{से} \hi{शाम} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दस} \hi{बजे} \hi{से} \hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item what changed in the frame between days and hours (nothing)
  \item the two packages inside the clock span
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the span frame change when the units change? (No.) What sits between \textbf{\hi{दस}} and \textbf{\hi{से}}? (\textbf{\hi{बजे}}.) Which direction does the phrase grow in? (Rightwards, one word at a time.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭren]{\hi{ट्रेन} — a word that travelled with the thing}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-train}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{by bus}. Say \emph{station}. You have had a station for a while without a second way of reaching it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{ट्रेन}}
\textbf{\hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से}} — by train.

\begin{cousinweb}
Both of your vehicles are borrowed words, and they are borrowed the same way:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{from} & \textbf{by …} \\
\midrule
\hi{बस} & English \emph{bus} & \hi{बस} \hi{से} \\
\hi{ट्रेन} & English \emph{train} & \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{\hi{से}} that makes them \emph{by bus} and \emph{by train} is the one already taught for means — the same word that says \emph{from}, and that this chapter has been using for the start of a span.

Look at the first letter. \textbf{\hi{ट}} is the retroflex one, made with the tongue curled back — and it is used here because English \emph{t} in \emph{train} sounds, to a Hindi ear, much more like \textbf{\hi{ट}} than like the dental \textbf{\hi{त}}. That is the regular habit for English loanwords, and it is why \textbf{\hi{ट्रेन}} and not \textbf{\hi{त्रेन}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a word Hindi also has its own name for}]
Hindi does have an inherited word for a railway train, and an A1 reader will still meet \textbf{\hi{ट्रेन}} far more often — on a board, in a timetable, in the middle of an ordinary sentence about getting to work.

Learn the borrowed one first because it is the one that is said. The other is worth recognising later, when reading formal notices is the task.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बस} \hi{से}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word that makes both of them mean \emph{by}
  \item why the first letter is the curled-back one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{by train}? (\textbf{\hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से}}.) Which \textbf{\hi{त}}-family letter does it start with, and why? (The retroflex \textbf{\hi{ट}}, because that is what English \emph{t} sounds like here.) What else has \textbf{\hi{से}} done in this chapter? (Marked the start of a span.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nahīṁ kī jagah]{nahīṁ kī jagah — how much the negative takes back}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-se-nahin}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{by bus} and \emph{by train}. Now imagine somebody has guessed the first one and you need to give them the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: X \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, Y \hi{से}}
\textbf{\hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से।}} — Not by bus — by train.

\textbf{\hi{नहीं}} stands between the two options, and the one it rejects is the one \textbf{before} it.

\subsection*{The two words}
Read the frame as three beats:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{beat} & \textbf{contents} \\
\midrule
1 & the wrong option, with its own \textbf{\hi{से}} \\
2 & \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} \\
3 & the right option, with its own \textbf{\hi{से}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Each option keeps its marker.} That is the part to watch, because English drops the second one — \emph{not by bus, by train} has one \emph{by}, and Hindi has two \textbf{\hi{से}}. A sentence with only one \textbf{\hi{से}} is not this frame.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what \hi{नहीं} is negating}]
In every sentence so far, \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} has stood in front of the verb and denied the whole thing. Here it stands after a noun-plus-postposition and denies \textbf{only that phrase}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what is denied} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
the whole sentence & \hi{मैं} \hi{नहीं} \hi{जाता} \\
one option in it & \hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the position of \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} tells a reader how much of the sentence is being taken back — and getting it wrong turns a correction into a refusal. The English speaker's instinct is to reach for a word like \emph{but}; \textbf{this frame has no word in the middle beyond the negative itself}, and the comma carries the pause.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{बस} \hi{से}\textquotedblright{} — the correction the other way round
  \item which option \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} rejects, the one before or the one after
  \item how many times \textbf{\hi{से}} appears (twice)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which option does \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} deny? (The one before it.) How many \textbf{\hi{से}} does the frame need? (Two — one per option.) What does the position of \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} tell you in general? (How much of the sentence is being denied.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[se kī tālikā]{se kī tālikā — five jobs, one word}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-repaso-safar}



\begin{quote}
Name two things \textbf{\hi{से}} has done before this chapter, and the word that has now joined it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: everything \hi{से} does}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{job} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
from a place & \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{से} \\
by a means & \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \\
measured against & \hi{बच्चे} \hi{से} \hi{बड़ा} \\
the start of a span & \hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \\
one option in a correction & \hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five jobs and no change of form. \textbf{\hi{से} never bends}, whatever it is doing and whatever stands in front of it — unlike \textbf{\hi{का}}, which had to become \textbf{\hi{के}} the moment another word followed.

The reason is worth keeping: \textbf{\hi{का}} is a possessive and possessives agree, while \textbf{\hi{से}} is a plain postposition and has nothing to agree with.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the partner, and where it stands}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{span} & \textbf{start} & \textbf{stop} \\
\midrule
days & \hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} & \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक} \\
parts of a day & \hi{सुबह} \hi{से} & \hi{शाम} \hi{तक} \\
clock hours & \hi{दस} \hi{बजे} \hi{से} & \hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{तक}} can stand alone — \textbf{\hi{पाँच} \hi{बजे} \hi{तक}} needs no \textbf{\hi{से}}. \textbf{\hi{से}} can stand alone too. The pair is a choice, not a requirement.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one place two \hi{से} are compulsory}]
\textbf{\hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से।}}

English keeps one \emph{by} and lets it cover both halves. Hindi gives each option its own \textbf{\hi{से}}, because each option is a complete phrase in its own right and \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} sits between two complete phrases rather than inside one.

Count the \textbf{\hi{से}} when you read a correction. Two means a swap is being offered; one means something else is going on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{सुबह} \hi{से} \hi{शाम} \hi{तक}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the number of jobs \textbf{\hi{से}} now has (five)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\hi{से}} ever change its form? (No.) Does \textbf{\hi{तक}} need \textbf{\hi{से}}? (No.) How many \textbf{\hi{से}} does a correction need? (Two.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maiṁ ṭren se jāūṁgā]{\hi{मैं} \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \hi{जाऊँगा} — reading a correction in a paper}

\label{lesson:HI-C94-sintesis-safar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I will do}. Then say the verb for going. The future ending you learned on one verb attaches to any stem, and this is the sentence that wants it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{speaker} & \textbf{Hindi} \\
\midrule
A & \hi{आप} \hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{जाएँगे}? \\
B & \hi{मैं} \hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \hi{जाऊँगा।} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

B does two things at once: rejects A's guess and supplies the replacement, in one sentence with one verb at the end of it.

\subsection*{How to answer}
Find \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} first. Everything before it is what is being denied; everything after it up to the verb is what replaces it.

Then check the count: \textbf{two \hi{से}} means a swap. An item that asks \emph{how will B travel} is answered by the phrase \textbf{after} the negative, and the commonest wrong answer is the phrase before it — which is exactly why the paper prints the rejected option first.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the chapter in one sentence}]
\textbf{\hi{से}} marks a start and \textbf{\hi{तक}} marks a stop, and between them they carry both a week and a working day:

\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक} \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \hi{जाऊँगा।}}

Two \textbf{\hi{से}} in that sentence, doing \textbf{different} jobs — the first opens a span, the second names a means. Neither is a mistake, and telling them apart is a matter of looking for a \textbf{\hi{तक}} further along.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{बस} \hi{से} \hi{नहीं}, \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \hi{जाऊँगा}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{सोमवार} \hi{से} \hi{शुक्रवार} \hi{तक} \hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से} \hi{जाऊँगा}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which phrase answers \emph{how will B travel}
  \item how to tell a span \textbf{\hi{से}} from a means \textbf{\hi{से}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which side of \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} holds the true answer? (The side after it.) What tells you a \textbf{\hi{से}} opens a span? (A \textbf{\hi{तक}} further along.) What is \emph{by train}? (\textbf{\hi{ट्रेन} \hi{से}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
